title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
text:
Forest managers using retention forestry need information on regeneration and fuel development to design productive stands in fire-adapted ecosystems. We analyzed 10-year remeasurement data from the Redwood Multiaged Experiment in Jackson Demonstration State Forest, California. The experiment compared group selection, aggregated retention, and low- and high-density dispersed retention treatments and measured regeneration, sprout growth, and surface fuel loading.
Redwood regeneration responded strongly to increasing canopy openness, whereas tanoak responses were more modest. Sprout-height findings will remain part of the main regeneration evidence. Fuel measurements describe conditions before and after precommercial thinning, including the PCT-associated contrast. The manuscript will evaluate how overstory retention affects regeneration while presenting fuel components in a form useful for integrated silviculture, fuels, and fire management.

title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
text:
Study area and design
The experiment is located in the Jackson Demonstration State Forest in coastal northern California. Four harvest treatments were replicated at four sites in 2012: group selection (GS), high-density dispersed retention (HD), high-density aggregated retention (HA), and low-density dispersed retention (LD). The retained-overstory treatments targeted post-harvest relative densities of 13% or 21%; group selection created a 1-ha opening with a lightly thinned buffer. These treatments were designed to examine alternative pathways for developing multiaged redwood stands (Berrill & O’Hara, 2009; Reineke, 1933).
Ten years after harvest, regeneration plots and fuel transects were established within each 0.2-ha treatment macro plot. Regeneration measurements characterized redwood, tanoak, and Douglas-fir; fuel transects characterized dead surface fuels and live vegetation. The plots were remeasured after precommercial thinning, which released selected conifers from competing trees and shrubs.

title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
text:
Analysis
The final publication methods will identify the regeneration models retained from the thesis and the revised fuel-component specifications separately. They will define the phase-specific fuel estimates and the PCT-associated contrast, including whether the sampling design supports a paired change analysis. Detailed sampling procedures, model diagnostics, and expanded comparisons will be retained as supplementary material where they are needed for reproducibility but not for interpretation of the main findings.
For the R-D04 fuel display, treatment- and phase-specific mean loads were estimated by averaging response-scale expectations, including modeled zeros, over an equally weighted grid of the four study-site contexts and analytically integrating over all fitted Gaussian random-intercept distributions. These estimates provide model-based reference means for comparable forest conditions; 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the delta method with the full parameter covariance, including uncertainty in random-effect variances. Mean woody standing-vegetation reduction was estimated as the pre-PCT minus post-PCT contrast from the matched repeated-phase model, with its joint covariance, and interpreted as a potential surface-fuel contribution.

title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
text:
Regeneration under varying overstory retention
The thesis results provide the starting material for basal area, understory density, and sprout-height summaries. At 10 years after harvest, redwood regeneration was greatest in the most open treatment and declined with greater overstory retention. Tanoak responses were comparatively modest. Redwood and tanoak sprout-height findings will remain in the main results; other species will be retained as descriptive context where useful rather than as dedicated main-text analyses. The final figures and summaries will retain these results only after the publication presentation and modeling review are complete.

title: Regeneration and fuel loading with varying overstory retention in redwood stands
text:
Fuel conditions as reference values
Fuel conditions are reported second to support interpretation of the silvicultural treatments and to characterize the management-relevant transition before and after precommercial thinning. The thesis found comparatively few treatment differences in fine dead fuels before precommercial thinning, whereas vegetation fuels were greater in more open treatments. The publication analysis will separate fuel components that were previously combined, report phase- specific estimates and uncertainty, and evaluate the PCT-associated contrast. Treatment comparisons will be retained where they clarify PCT or retained- overstory implications.

R-D04 fuel inventory draft
The following display is a draft pending review. It is included here so the figure, caption, and eventual fuel Results narrative can be reviewed in their manuscript context. Its estimates have not yet been converted into the R-T03 Results narrative.








Figure 1: Fuel components by retention treatment before and after precommercial thinning (PCT). Points are site-standardized mean loads from AIC-leading models, integrated over all fitted random effects and including modeled zeros; ranges are 95% confidence intervals for the means. Study sites receive equal weights. Orange denotes pre-PCT and blue denotes post-PCT for the six components measured in both phases. Litter and duff are pre-PCT only. The woody vegetation-difference panel is the pre-PCT minus post-PCT mean contrast from the joint matched woody phase model, with its pre/post covariance. It is an inferred potential surface-fuel contribution, not direct slash load. Panel-specific y-scales are used.

title: Publication manuscript development
text:
This standalone Quarto project is the publication-development workspace for the Redwood Multiaged Experiment. It is intentionally separate from the legacy profile-driven project in analysis/.
The manuscript will retain the thesis as its substantive starting point while being reorganized around a regeneration-first pyro-silviculture narrative. Fuel conditions will be reported as disaggregated pre- and post-PCT reference values, including the PCT-associated contrast, to inform integrated silvicultural, fuels, fire, and potential modeling applications.
The workflow page is the authoritative planning view: it summarizes every task’s objective, constraints, status, decisions, generated artifacts, and review-ready outputs. Background source maps and detailed historical records remain linked from the relevant task rather than competing as separate planning queues.

title: Publication manuscript development
text:
Working boundaries
This project does not execute or alter the thesis-era analyses. Future publication-specific derived data, model objects, figures, and tables will be written to ../analysis/outputs/publication/. Shared raw data, utilities, figures, and bibliography resources remain in their established repository locations until a stable shared interface is deliberately extracted.

title: Publication workflow and review queue
text: This page is the working index for publication development. Each task is tracked like a small issue: it begins with an objective and guardrails, records the decisions and artifacts produced while it is open, and ends either in a reviewable manuscript product or a completed analytical record. The manuscript is developed backwards from the results displays: figures and tables → results → methods → discussion → introduction → abstract → title. This order adapts the “write backwards” approach described by Montagnes, Montagnes, and Yang (2022).

title: Publication workflow and review queue
text:
How to use this queue
Each task has a short proposal below it before any work is done. Review and edit that proposal, then move the task through this sequence:
Direction for review → Approved to execute → In progress → Pending review → Accepted (or Revision requested) → Complete.
“Queued” means the task is deliberately decomposed and ready to be proposed; it is not yet authorized for execution. “Completed — analytical record” means the reproducible work is preserved, while a decision explicitly marked provisional still awaits scientific review. Page targets are working allocations for the main manuscript, not a journal requirement.

title: Publication workflow and review queue
text:
Fuel-analysis preparation

F-01 — fuel-component separation and model exploration
Status: Completed — analytical record.

Original objective and guardrails
Create publication-only fuel components that preserve the thesis analyses while making the pre- and post-PCT data usable as distinct reference phases. Retain the fixed experimental-design random-intercept structure; record every model candidate and diagnostic; do not treat an AIC leader as a selected model.

Thesis notebooks, raw data, and thesis-era .rda objects remain unchanged.
Pre-PCT litter and duff are separated using the Finney–Martin model-3 forest-floor partition; post-PCT litter and duff are deliberately omitted because their boundary is not currently defensible.
Woody and herbaceous vegetation are separate in both phases.
The primary PCT contrast is matched-transect pre-PCT minus post-PCT woody standing vegetation—an inferred potential surface-fuel contribution, not a direct slash-load measurement.



Decisions made








Decision area
Recorded decision
Why it matters for the publication display




Reporting phases
Show pre- and post-PCT values as distinct phases.
Avoids treating the contrast as automatically causal.


Forest floor
Report modeled litter and duff only before PCT.
Prevents a misleading post-PCT forest-floor estimate.


Vegetation
Keep woody and herbaceous components separate.
Allows the PCT-related standing-woody change to remain visible.


PCT estimand
Use matched pre minus post woody standing vegetation.
Clearly labels the management contrast and its limitation.


Model selection
Preserve all candidates; leaders are provisional pending scientific review.
Keeps model choice auditable instead of hiding it in a final table.

title: Publication workflow and review queue
text:
Results displays

R-D04 — fuel phase and PCT display
Status: Complete. The figure has been generated from the current AIC-leading fitted publication models. Its position in the register is an organizational sequence, not a required execution order relative to R-D02 or R-D03.
The prediction and interpretation review below now compares the thesis and R-D04 estimands, demonstrates both prediction implementations, and records the Methods wording. The figure now uses random-effect-integrated mean loads throughout and the joint woody phase model for the displayed pre-minus-post mean change. The completed display and its model assumptions are recorded below.

Objective
Produce a compact, reviewable full-inventory figure (and caption) from the current AIC-leading fitted publication models. Use nine panels: paired pre-/ post-PCT estimates for 1-, 10-, 100-, and 1,000-hour fuels plus woody and herbaceous vegetation; pre-PCT-only panels for litter and duff; and a separate matched woody-vegetation-difference panel (pre-PCT minus post-PCT). The figure must retain uncertainty, retained-overstory treatment context, and the qualified interpretation of the vegetation-difference estimand.


Constraints and starting material

Use the saved fitted models identified as AIC leaders in the F-01 model-selection register. Their diagnostic/scientific review remains visible through the figure-review decision rather than blocking draft generation.
Integrate over all fitted random effects for a consistent mean-load interpretation, with equal study-site weights. Derive woody mean change from the same joint phase model as the woody load panels, retaining its pre/post covariance.
Retain the thesis visual grammar—model estimate point with a colored 95% CI range—for the six paired panels. Label pre-PCT-only litter and duff panels explicitly; do not imply a post-PCT zero or estimate.
Plot the matched woody vegetation difference separately with a zero reference line. It is an inferred potential surface-fuel contribution, not direct slash load, so it must not be styled as another phase estimate.
Use panel-specific y-scales and a 3 × 3 layout to keep the broad load range legible. Keep full model registries, diagnostics, and pairwise comparisons in linked artifacts rather than adding them to the figure.



Suggested deliverables

A nine-panel model-estimate figure: six paired phase panels, litter, duff, and the matched woody vegetation-difference panel.
A publication caption and a short Results paragraph, both marked Pending review when draft-ready.
A linked table or CSV of complete phase-by-treatment model estimates and a link to the model-selection register used for the draft.



Completed output








Figure 1: R-D04 full fuel inventory by retention treatment. Points are site-standardized mean loads from AIC-leading models, integrated over all fitted random effects and including modeled zeros; ranges are 95% confidence intervals for the means. Study sites receive equal weights. Orange denotes pre-PCT and blue denotes post-PCT for the six components measured in both phases. Litter and duff are pre-PCT only. The woody vegetation-difference panel is the pre-PCT minus post-PCT mean contrast from the joint matched woody phase model, with its pre/post covariance. It is an inferred potential surface-fuel contribution, not direct slash load. Panel-specific y-scales are used.





Generated artifacts for this review are analysis/outputs/publication/fuel/figures/rd04-fuel-phase-pct-inventory.png, analysis/outputs/publication/fuel/tables/rd04-fuel-model-estimates.csv, and analysis/outputs/publication/fuel/manifests/rd04-figure-provenance.yml. The figure uses the AIC-leading models documented in the rendered F-01 model-review register above. It is also available in the working manuscript for review in context.

# Generate the R-D04 inventory with a consistent integrated mean-load estimand.
# Run from analysis/: Rscript scripts/publication/fuel/08-generate-rd04-integrated-figure.R
script_argument <- grep("^--file=", commandArgs(FALSE), value = TRUE)
stopifnot(length(script_argument) == 1L)
script_dir <- dirname(normalizePath(sub("^--file=", "", script_argument)))
analysis_root <- normalizePath(file.path(script_dir, "..", "..", ".."))
source(file.path(script_dir, "00-fuel-config.R"))
source(file.path(script_dir, "rd04-inference-utils.R"))
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(glmmTMB)
  library(patchwork)
  library(readr)
})

models_dir <- file.path(paths$output, "models")
figures_dir <- file.path(paths$output, "figures")
tables_dir <- file.path(paths$output, "tables")

spec <- tibble::tribble(
  ~model_id, ~component, ~phase,
  "prepct_onehr_disp_treatment", "1-hour fuel", "prepct",
  "postpct_onehr_base", "1-hour fuel", "postpct",
  "prepct_tenhr_base", "10-hour fuel", "prepct",
  "postpct_tenhr_base", "10-hour fuel", "postpct",
  "prepct_hundhr_base", "100-hour fuel", "prepct",
  "postpct_hundhr_zi_treatment_site_disp_treatment_site_interaction", "100-hour fuel", "postpct",
  "prepct_thoushr_base", "1,000-hour fuel", "prepct",
  "postpct_thoushr_zi_treatment", "1,000-hour fuel", "postpct",
  "woody_phase_zigamma_ziphase_disp1", "Woody vegetation", NA_character_,
  "prepct_herbaceous_vegetation_base", "Herbaceous vegetation", "prepct",
  "postpct_herbaceous_vegetation_base", "Herbaceous vegetation", "postpct",
  "prepct_litter_disp_treatment", "Litter (pre-PCT only)", "prepct",
  "prepct_duff_base", "Duff (pre-PCT only)", "prepct"
)
selection <- read_csv(file.path(paths$manifests, "model-selection-log.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(all(spec$model_id %in% selection$provisional_aic_leader),
          all(file.exists(file.path(models_dir, paste0(spec$model_id, ".rds")))))

summarize_integrated <- function(s, component, model_id, phase = NULL, difference = FALSE) {
  prediction <- custom_integrated(s)
  # Means use log-delta intervals; signed differences use response-scale ones.
  low <- if (difference) prediction$estimate - qnorm(.975) * prediction$se else
    prediction$estimate * exp(-qnorm(.975) * prediction$se / prediction$estimate)
  high <- if (difference) prediction$estimate + qnorm(.975) * prediction$se else
    prediction$estimate * exp(qnorm(.975) * prediction$se / prediction$estimate)
  labels <- s$avg$labels
  phase_values <- if (difference) rep("Vegetation difference", nrow(labels)) else {
    values <- if ("phase" %in% names(labels)) as.character(labels$phase) else rep(phase, nrow(labels))
    stopifnot(all(values %in% c("prepct", "postpct")))
    ifelse(values == "prepct", "Pre-PCT", "Post-PCT")
  }
  tibble(component = component, phase = phase_values,
         treatment = as.character(labels$treatment), estimate = prediction$estimate,
         se = prediction$se, lcl = low, ucl = high, model_id = model_id,
         estimand = if (difference) "integrated matched woody mean difference (pre-PCT minus post-PCT)" else
           "site-standardized random-effect-integrated expected load",
         interval_method = if (difference) "response-scale delta method with joint phase covariance" else
           "log-scale delta method for integrated mean",
         random_intercept_variance = s$variance)
}

phase_estimates <- list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(spec))) {
  item <- spec[i, ]
  model <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, paste0(item$model_id, ".rds")))
  phase_arg <- if (is.na(item$phase)) NULL else item$phase
  s <- integration_setup(model, reference_grid(model, phase_arg))
  stopifnot(all(rowSums(s$avg$A > 0) == 4L))
  phase_estimates[[i]] <- summarize_integrated(s, item$component, item$model_id, phase_arg)
  if (item$component == "Woody vegetation") {
    difference_component <- summarize_integrated(
      woody_change_setup(s), "Woody vegetation difference (pre-PCT minus post-PCT)",
      item$model_id, difference = TRUE)
  }
}
estimates <- bind_rows(bind_rows(phase_estimates), difference_component) |>
  mutate(
    treatment = factor(treatment, levels = c("gs", "ld", "ha", "hd")),
    phase = factor(phase, levels = c("Pre-PCT", "Post-PCT", "Vegetation difference")),
    component = factor(component, levels = c(
      "1-hour fuel", "10-hour fuel", "100-hour fuel", "1,000-hour fuel",
      "Woody vegetation", "Herbaceous vegetation", "Litter (pre-PCT only)",
      "Duff (pre-PCT only)", "Woody vegetation difference (pre-PCT minus post-PCT)"))
  ) |>
  arrange(component, phase, treatment)
stopifnot(nrow(estimates) == 60L, all(is.finite(estimates$estimate)),
          all(is.finite(estimates$se)), all(estimates$se >= 0),
          all(estimates$lcl <= estimates$estimate), all(estimates$ucl >= estimates$estimate))
# Every displayed woody change must equal the plotted pre-minus-post means.
woody_means <- filter(estimates, component == "Woody vegetation")
for (trt in levels(estimates$treatment)) {
  pre <- filter(woody_means, treatment == trt, phase == "Pre-PCT")$estimate
  post <- filter(woody_means, treatment == trt, phase == "Post-PCT")$estimate
  delta <- filter(difference_component, treatment == trt)$estimate
  stopifnot(abs(pre - post - delta) < 1e-8)
}
write_csv(estimates, file.path(tables_dir, "rd04-fuel-model-estimates.csv"))
difference_component <- filter(estimates, phase == "Vegetation difference")

phase_colors <- c("Pre-PCT" = "#C96F38", "Post-PCT" = "#3F51B5")
phase_position <- position_dodge(width = 0.52)

phase_panel <- function(component_name) {
  data <- filter(estimates, .data$component == .env$component_name)
  ggplot(data, aes(x = treatment, y = estimate, ymin = lcl, ymax = ucl, color = phase, group = phase)) +
    geom_linerange(linewidth = 2.2, position = phase_position) +
    geom_point(shape = 21, fill = "black", color = "white", size = 2.5, stroke = 0.6, position = phase_position) +
    scale_color_manual(values = phase_colors, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = c(gs = "GS", ld = "LD", ha = "HA", hd = "HD")) +
    labs(title = component_name, x = NULL, y = expression(Load ~ (Mg %.% ha^-1))) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "none"
    )
}

difference_panel <- function() {
  data <- difference_component
  ggplot(data, aes(x = treatment, y = estimate, ymin = lcl, ymax = ucl)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray45", linewidth = 0.45) +
    geom_linerange(color = "#5A4A42", linewidth = 2.2) +
    geom_point(shape = 21, fill = "black", color = "white", size = 2.5, stroke = 0.6) +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = c(gs = "GS", ld = "LD", ha = "HA", hd = "HD")) +
    labs(
      title = "Woody vegetation difference\n(pre-PCT minus post-PCT)",
      x = NULL,
      y = expression(Load ~ difference ~ (Mg %.% ha^-1))
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

component_order <- levels(estimates$component)
plots <- lapply(component_order[1:8], phase_panel)
plots[[9]] <- difference_panel()
figure <- wrap_plots(plots, ncol = 3, guides = "collect") +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect")

ggsave(file.path(figures_dir, "rd04-fuel-phase-pct-inventory.png"), figure, width = 10.5, height = 10, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

Prediction and interpretation review
Implemented approach: use study-standardized, population-averaged expected loads as the baseline for mean fuel loading in comparable systems. Integrate over the fitted random-intercept distributions and include modeled zeros, with equal weights for the four study-site contexts. Retain the historical zero-random-effect predictions as a clearly labeled reference/sensitivity summary in the audit. R-D04 now uses this integrated interpretation throughout, with woody mean change derived from the joint phase model; the fitted load models remain provisional pending scientific review. The original generator has been retired in favor of 08-generate-rd04-integrated-figure.R.

marginaleffects passes the random-effect arguments to the fitted model’s prediction method. Its by argument and avg_predictions() average the predictions supplied to them; they do not change zero-effect predictions into random-effect-integrated predictions. This distinction follows the mixed-model vignette, the prediction reference, and the distinction between observed-group averaging and new-group integration in the Bayesian vignette.
For glmmTMB, arbitrary formulas selecting random effects in re.form are not supported. Selected grouping variables can instead be set to NA, but this is unsuitable when a variable is also required as a fixed predictor: site, for example, must remain defined for the post-PCT 100-hour model’s zero component. allow.new.levels = TRUE permits new grouping IDs; it does not request integration over their possible effects. See the model’s prediction documentation.
Two different uses of “conditional” also need separating: type = "conditional" requests the conditional-distribution mean, whereas re.form controls conditioning on random effects. For these zero-inflated Gamma models, type = "response" returns \((1-p_0)\mu_+\), including the modeled probability of zero, while type = "conditional" returns \(\mu_+\). Dispersion parameters affect variability and estimation but are not additional multipliers of this response mean. Gamma sampling variability should not receive a lognormal residual-variance correction.


Alignment of the thesis code and interpretation
The controlling Results function is marginaleffects_to_emmeans() in analysis/thesis/results.qmd: both predictions and comparisons use re.form = NA. For fuel loads, its pre- and post-PCT calls use tidyr::expand(data, treatment, site), giving equal site weights. Passing the predictions and pairwise-difference standard errors into emmeans::emmobj() changes their representation, not their underlying estimand. The earlier re.form = NULL exploratory basal-area plots in regen_visualize.qmd are not the calls controlling the thesis Results.







Thesis statement or presentation
Assessment




Methods: predictions incorporate all components and average over random effects to obtain population means
Partly aligned: response predictions can include the zero component, but the wrapper sets random effects to zero before averaging. The random effects were not integrated out.


Methods: estimates apply to equal proportions of similar sites, specifically north- and south-facing aspects
Equal site weights are explicit for fuel grids. Zeroing site random effects does not reproduce an aspect mixture on a nonlinear response scale; aspect was not a fixed adjustment variable. Transport requires an exchangeability assumption beyond the prediction settings.


Fuel Results: “expected value” and “estimated marginal means”
Valid if identified as site-standardized expectations at zero random effects. Too broad if read as arithmetic population-average loads across forest heterogeneity.


Discussion: compare “average” loads with other forest studies
State whether each value is an observed mean, a zero-effect reference, or an integrated model mean, and check component definitions and sampling protocols. These quantities are not interchangeable.


Post-PCT caption: vegetation difference “represents slash fuels recruited to the forest floor”
Overstates the measurement: standing-vegetation reduction is an inferred potential contribution, not measured slash deposition. R-D04’s qualified caption is better aligned.


Results: pre/post estimates are not statistically comparable because model structures differ
Different structures alone do not prevent comparison. Formal phase differences need an explicit common estimand and their covariance, accounting for pairing. Separate phase CIs do not supply a paired change test.


Discussion/conclusions: PCT “resulted in” or “generated” the observed dead-fuel changes
The observed transition supports association; attributing all change to PCT requires the design/time assumptions. No unthinned contemporaneous comparison is used by these predictions.



The same wrapper controls regeneration and sprout Results. Basal area, Douglas-fir counts, and year-10 height use nonlinear links, so zero-effect and integrated means can differ there too. Height increment uses an identity link; integration over mean-zero random effects leaves its expected value unchanged, for a fixed covariate distribution. The Results grids also vary: treatment height-increment summaries explicitly balance years, whereas the by-year analysis uses newdata = NULL and averages within observed species/year cells. Those are different standardization choices and should be described separately. The fuel integration code below is deliberately restricted to its audited model structures; it is not a general-purpose replacement for those other analyses.
One numerical provenance issue also deserves attention: the Discussion reports about 42 Mg/ha of pre-PCT 1,000-hour fuel. Reproducing the Results wrapper on the saved thesis models gives an equal-treatment reference mean of 32.63 Mg/ha. The Discussion value may be an observed summary, but it should not be presented as the grand mean of these particular model predictions without a separate source. The audit preserves all reproduced thesis fuel estimates.

The original R-D04 and thesis fuel Results used the same zero-random-effect target and equal-site weighting. Implemented target and worked demonstration
For a treatment \(t\), phase \(h\), and equally weighted site contexts \(s\), define
\[
M_{th} = \frac{1}{4}\sum_{s=1}^{4}
  E_b\!\left[(1-p_{0,sth})\exp\{x_{sth}^{\mathsf T}\beta + z^{\mathsf T}b\}\right].
\]
The audited load models have independent Gaussian random intercepts only in the conditional model and no random effects in the zero component. Thus, with \(v=\sum_k\sigma_k^2\) across all modeled random-intercept levels,
\[
M_{th}=\exp(v/2)\,
\frac{1}{4}\sum_{s=1}^{4}(1-p_{0,sth})\exp(x_{sth}^{\mathsf T}\beta).
\]
This is exact under the fitted model, not a generic bias-correction option. The same multiplier across treatments within a fitted load model preserves ratios and rankings, while changing absolute loads and differences. Inference must still propagate uncertainty in the multiplier; old p-values and standard errors should not simply be carried over.
The separate Student-t difference model was replaced in the display by the integrated joint phase-model contrast so that woody change equals the difference between the displayed arithmetic mean loads. Its uncertainty retains the joint pre/post covariance, keeping the change estimate consistent with the matched design and the mean-load interpretation of the other panels.
For post-PCT 100-hour fuel, “site-standardized” specifically retains an equal mixture of the four fitted zero-process site contexts. Integration of the random intercepts cannot create a zero-process coefficient for a fifth site. The baseline therefore concerns comparable contexts, not a fitted prediction for any arbitrary new forest. Four sites also provide limited information about the site-variance distribution. A regional mean, or an explicitly 50:50 aspect-standardized mean, would need a justified target distribution and sufficient covariate information to support that standardization.
The demonstration holds fitted load models fixed and changes the estimand; woody change now uses their joint phase model. Selected GS examples below show why the distinction matters (Mg/ha). The intervals describe uncertainty in the integrated mean, not variation in a new forest or transect.

The implementation in 07-audit-rd04-inference.R demonstrates both routes:

Historical reference target: marginaleffects::avg_predictions(model, newdata = grid, by = ..., type = "response", re.form = NA) agrees with predict() followed by explicit matrix averaging. The custom variance is A %*% prediction$cov.fit %*% t(A).
Implemented integrated target: a nonlinear functional supplied to marginaleffects::hypotheses() averages the response means after analytic integration. A separate custom implementation derives its gradient and calculates G %*% V %*% t(G). Both use the full covariance of the fitted nonrandom parameters, including zero-model coefficients, log random-effect standard deviations, and their cross-covariances. Merely multiplying an avg_predictions() interval by exp(v/2) would omit uncertainty in \(v\).

The hypotheses documentation supports nonlinear functionals and supplied covariance matrices. Here the full parameter table is supplied explicitly because ordinary fixed-coefficient prediction covariance alone does not include the integration multiplier’s variance. These are asymptotic delta-method intervals, conditional on the chosen models and the reference grid. They do not include model-selection or fuel-component-derivation uncertainty. Refitted parametric bootstrap intervals are a useful final sensitivity check, particularly for herbaceous loads with large variance corrections and only four sites.
Verification: the audit checks all 60 historical comparison cells for agreement of reference point estimates and SEs, integrated point estimates, and integrated SEs; the latter agree within a relative/absolute tolerance of \(10^{-4}\). It checks the integration multiplier against numerical quadrature, the matrix predictions against predict.glmmTMB(), and the retired script’s checksum before and after the run. It additionally verifies all four woody mean contrasts with cross-phase covariance and reproduces the 48 thesis fuel reference estimates. Outputs and the R/package session record are in analysis/outputs/publication/fuel/inference-audit/.

# Keep valid nested identifiers from one observed row per site/treatment/phase.
# These identifiers do not contribute fitted random effects when re.form=NA.
reference_grid <- function(model, phase = NULL) {
  keys <- intersect(c("site", "treatment", "phase"), names(model$frame))
  grid <- distinct(model$frame, across(all_of(keys)), .keep_all = TRUE)
  if (!is.null(phase) && "phase" %in% keys) grid <- filter(grid, .data$phase == .env$phase)
  counts <- count(grid, treatment)
  stopifnot(length(unique(counts$n)) == 1L)
  grid
}

# A maps row predictions to equally weighted site means. A V A' retains every
# cross-site covariance; treating site predictions as independent is incorrect.
averaging_matrix <- function(grid) {
  keys <- intersect(c("treatment", "phase"), names(grid))
  labels <- distinct(grid, across(all_of(keys)))
  A <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(labels)), function(i) {
    keep <- Reduce(`&`, lapply(keys, function(k) grid[[k]] == labels[[k]][i]))
    as.numeric(keep) / sum(keep)
  }, numeric(nrow(grid))))
  list(A = A, labels = labels)
}

custom_reference <- function(model, grid) {
  p <- predict(model, newdata = grid, type = "response", re.form = NA,
               allow.new.levels = TRUE, se.fit = TRUE, cov.fit = TRUE)
  avg <- averaging_matrix(grid)
  transform(avg$labels, estimate = as.vector(avg$A %*% p$fit),
            std.error = sqrt(diag(avg$A %*% p$cov.fit %*% t(avg$A))))
}

# Exact integration for THESE models: independent Gaussian random intercepts in
# the conditional model, log/identity link, no random effects in the zero model.
# This deliberately fails on slopes, correlated effects, offsets, or other links.
integration_setup <- function(model, grid) {
  vc <- VarCorr(model)
  stopifnot(length(vc$zi) == 0L, length(vc$disp) == 0L,
            all(vapply(vc$cond, function(x) identical(dim(x), c(1L, 1L)), logical(1))))
  X <- model.matrix(delete.response(terms(formula(model, fixed.only = TRUE))), grid)
  Z <- model.matrix(formula(model, component = "zi", fixed.only = TRUE), grid)
  par <- model$fit$par
  ib <- which(names(par) == "beta")
  iz <- which(names(par) == "betazi")
  it <- which(names(par) == "theta")
  stopifnot(ncol(X) == length(ib), ncol(Z) == length(iz),
            length(it) == length(vc$cond), model$sdr$pdHess,
            isTRUE(all.equal(unname(par), unname(model$sdr$par.fixed))),
            is.null(model.offset(model$frame)),
            family(model)$link %in% c("log", "identity"))
  variance <- sum(vapply(vc$cond, function(x) x[1, 1], numeric(1)))
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(variance, sum(exp(2 * par[it])), tolerance = 1e-8)))
  list(X = X, Z = Z, par = par, V = model$sdr$cov.fixed,
       ib = ib, iz = iz, it = it, link = family(model)$link,
       avg = averaging_matrix(grid), variance = variance)
}

# Independent analytic derivatives for the custom delta-method implementation.
custom_integrated <- function(s) {
  eta <- drop(s$X %*% s$par[s$ib])
  pzero <- if (length(s$iz)) plogis(drop(s$Z %*% s$par[s$iz])) else rep(0, length(eta))
  if (s$link == "log") {
    mu <- exp(eta + s$variance / 2) * (1 - pzero)
    D <- matrix(0, nrow(s$X), length(s$par))
    D[, s$ib] <- mu * s$X
    if (length(s$iz)) D[, s$iz] <- -mu * pzero * s$Z
    D[, s$it] <- outer(mu, exp(2 * s$par[s$it]))
  } else {
    stopifnot(length(s$iz) == 0L)
    mu <- eta
    D <- matrix(0, nrow(s$X), length(s$par))
    D[, s$ib] <- s$X
  }
  G <- s$avg$A %*% D
  list(estimate = drop(s$avg$A %*% mu),
       se = sqrt(pmax(0, diag(G %*% s$V %*% t(G)))), G = G)
}

# Contrast the same matched model's integrated phase means, retaining their
# covariance through a single gradient and the full parameter covariance.
woody_change_setup <- function(s) {
  labels <- s$avg$labels
  stopifnot(all(c("phase", "treatment") %in% names(labels)),
            setequal(unique(as.character(labels$phase)), c("prepct", "postpct")))
  treatments <- unique(as.character(labels$treatment))
  C <- t(vapply(treatments, function(trt) {
    stopifnot(sum(labels$treatment == trt & labels$phase == "prepct") == 1L,
              sum(labels$treatment == trt & labels$phase == "postpct") == 1L)
    as.numeric(labels$treatment == trt) * ifelse(labels$phase == "prepct", 1, -1)
  }, numeric(nrow(labels))))
  s$avg$A <- C %*% s$avg$A
  s$avg$labels <- data.frame(treatment = treatments)
  s
}

# marginaleffects does the nonlinear delta method on a supplied full parameter
# table, including theta (log SDs), not just the conditional fixed coefficients.
# avg_predictions(re.form=NA) alone does NOT integrate over random effects.
marginaleffects_integrated <- function(s) {
  parameters <- data.frame(term = paste0("p", seq_along(s$par)),
                           estimate = unname(s$par))
  functional <- function(x) {
    b <- x$estimate
    eta <- drop(s$X %*% b[s$ib])
    pzero <- if (length(s$iz)) plogis(drop(s$Z %*% b[s$iz])) else rep(0, length(eta))
    mu <- if (s$link == "log") exp(eta + sum(exp(2 * b[s$it])) / 2) * (1 - pzero) else eta
    data.frame(term = seq_len(nrow(s$avg$labels)), estimate = drop(s$avg$A %*% mu))
  }
  marginaleffects::hypotheses(parameters, hypothesis = functional, vcov = s$V,
             numderiv = "fdcenter", conf_level = .95)
}

  summarise(load = mean(load), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = phase, values_from = load) |>
  mutate(observed_difference = prepct - postpct)
phase_change <- tibble(
  treatment = treatments, phase_model_difference = change$estimate,
  phase_model_difference_marginaleffects = change_me$estimate,
  se_custom = change$se, se_marginaleffects = change_me$std.error,
  lcl = change$estimate - qnorm(.975) * change$se,
  ucl = change$estimate + qnorm(.975) * change$se
) |>
  left_join(select(observed, treatment, observed_difference), by = "treatment") |>
  left_join(select(filter(audit, component == "Woody difference"), treatment,
                   separate_t_model_difference = integrated_custom), by = "treatment")
write_csv(phase_change, file.path(audit_dir, "woody-mean-change-comparison.csv"))

# Reproduce the thesis RESULTS grid on the original saved models, without
# executing or modifying any thesis notebook or changing its fitted models.
thesis <- new.env()
load(file.path(analysis_root, "fuel_modeling_round_3.rda"), envir = thesis)
thesis_results <- list()
for (phase in c("pre", "post")) {
  mods <- thesis$fuel_tmb[[phase]]
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(mods))) {
    m <- mods$mod[[i]]
    grid <- expand(mods$data[[i]], treatment, site)
    # Both historical approaches use observed, valid treatment/site pairs;
    # nested random-only identifiers are not crossed in the thesis fuel grid.
    stopifnot(nrow(anti_join(grid, distinct(m$frame, treatment, site),
                            by = c("treatment", "site"))) == 0L)
    p <- as.data.frame(avg_predictions(m, newdata = grid, by = "treatment",
                                      re.form = NA, type = "response"))
    thesis_results[[paste(phase, i)]] <- tibble(
      phase = paste0(phase, "pct"), thesis_class = as.character(mods$class[i]),
      treatment = as.character(p$treatment), thesis_reference = p$estimate,
      thesis_se = p$std.error, formula = deparse1(formula(m)),
      zero = deparse1(formula(m, component = "zi"))
    )
  }
}
thesis_results <- bind_rows(thesis_results)
write_csv(thesis_results, file.path(audit_dir, "thesis-reference-reproduction.csv"))
lookup <- c("1-hour" = "onehr", "10-hour" = "tenhr", "100-hour" = "hundhr", "1,000-hour" = "thoushr")
comparison <- audit |>
  filter(component %in% names(lookup)) |>
  mutate(thesis_class = unname(lookup[component])) |>
  left_join(select(thesis_results, phase, thesis_class, treatment, thesis_reference, thesis_se),
            by = c("phase", "thesis_class", "treatment")) |>
  mutate(reference_change = reference_custom - thesis_reference)
write_csv(comparison, file.path(audit_dir, "thesis-rd04-deadwood-comparison.csv"))

stopifnot(identical(original_hash, tools::md5sum(original_script)))
writeLines(c("R-D04 inference audit; existing fitted models; no refitting or model selection.",
             paste("Original script MD5:", unname(original_hash)),
             "Integrated SEs include beta, betazi, and log-SD covariance via sdr$cov.fixed.",
             "Intervals describe estimated means, not new-site or new-observation predictions.",
             capture.output(sessionInfo())), file.path(audit_dir, "session-info.txt"))
print(select(audit, component, phase, treatment, reference_custom, integrated_custom,
             original_se, corrected_reference_se), n = Inf)




Methods wording
For the implemented population-average baseline:

We estimated treatment- and phase-specific mean fuel loads by averaging response-scale expectations, including modeled zeros, over an equally weighted grid of the four study-site contexts and analytically integrating over all fitted Gaussian random-intercept distributions. These estimates provide model-based reference means for comparable forest conditions; 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the delta method with the full parameter covariance, including uncertainty in random-effect variances.

The matched-contrast qualification can be stated in its own Methods sentence:

Mean woody standing-vegetation reduction was estimated as the pre-PCT minus post-PCT contrast from the matched repeated-phase model, with its joint covariance, and interpreted as a potential surface-fuel contribution.

The former figure-and-table plan has been merged into this task; this is the authoritative action record for fuel-display development.

Inputs: thesis Results and fig-regen-ba-rw-to. Review product: one main figure, caption, and a decision on whether a compact estimates table adds information beyond annotations. Acceptance test: the display supports the main retention-response claim without a separate model-output table.

Results narratives

R-T01 — regeneration Results narrative
Status: Queued — after R-D02 acceptance. Proposal for review: write the basal-area/density result around the accepted regeneration display: state the primary redwood response to canopy openness, give concise tanoak context, and reserve other species for descriptive or supplemental treatment. Do not introduce interpretation that belongs in the Discussion.
Review product: 1–2-page Results subsection linked from the working manuscript. Acceptance test: every quantitative claim is visible in an accepted display or linked table.


R-T02 — sprout-height Results narrative
Status: Queued — after R-D03 acceptance. Proposal for review: report the accepted redwood and tanoak height/time findings in a distinct subsection; combine it with R-T01 only if one shared display and one take-home message make the combined result easier to read.
Review product: 1–1.5-page Results subsection. Acceptance test: it adds the sprout-development evidence without restating the regeneration basal-area/density result.


R-T03 — fuel Results narrative
Status: Queued — after R-D04 acceptance. Proposal for review: report phase-specific fuel conditions as reference values, then describe the qualified matched woody-standing-vegetation contrast. Retain treatment comparisons only where the accepted display makes their management role clear.
Review product: 1.5–2-page Results subsection, accepted fuel display, and linked detailed values. Acceptance test: it does not imply a direct slash-load measure or causal PCT effect beyond the reviewed design.

title: Publication workflow and review queue
text:
Methods

M-D01 — study design display
Status: Queued — Methods stage. Proposal for review: retain one legible study-design display that combines the study area/treatment layout and sampling logic, if that combination remains readable. Move the second map or layout to the supplement. It should orient the reader without duplicating the design table.
Inputs: thesis Methods Figures 2.1–2.2 and the current sampling-layout materials. Review product: candidate display, caption, accessibility text, and supplement disposition. Acceptance test: a reader can identify the four treatments, replication, and measurement phases without consulting the text.


M-01 — study area and experimental design
Status: Queued — after M-D01 acceptance. Proposal for review: retain the study setting, four treatments, replication, measurement timing, and PCT context needed to understand the accepted results. Use M-D01 and a compact design table to avoid reproducing procedural detail.
Review product: 1–1.5-page Methods subsection plus any compact table. Acceptance test: all variables and phases in accepted displays are traceable to the design.


M-02 — regeneration and sprout methods
Status: Queued — after R-T01/R-T02. Proposal for review: describe only the regeneration measurements and thesis-derived model/summaries retained in the accepted displays. Move expanded model specifications, comparisons, and secondary species detail to the supplement.
Review product: 1–1.5-page Methods subsection and supplement links. Acceptance test: a reader can reproduce the reported estimands without being asked to navigate unused thesis-era analyses.


M-03 — fuel methods and estimand
Status: Queued — after R-T03. Proposal for review: document the publication component definitions, phase boundary, matched woody contrast, uncertainty/model decision, and limits on causal language. Keep diagnostic detail in the linked F-01 artifacts and supplement.
Review product: 1–1.5-page Methods subsection. Acceptance test: the method wording exactly matches the accepted fuel caption and Results claims.

title: Publication workflow and review queue
text:
Discussion

D-01 — regeneration cohort discussion
Status: Queued. Proposal for review: interpret redwood and tanoak regeneration under retained overstory as evidence about developing a new cohort in multiaged redwood stands. Tighten the thesis discussion around the accepted basal-area/density evidence and its uncertainty.
Review product: 1.5–2-page Discussion subsection. Acceptance test: each inference follows an accepted Results claim and cited context.


D-02 — sprout development discussion
Status: Queued. Proposal for review: connect accepted sprout-height patterns to light, retention, and cohort development without duplicating D-01. Combine with D-01 only if the accepted results show one inseparable management message.
Review product: 1–1.5-page subsection. Acceptance test: it explains why the height result matters beyond the basal-area/density result.


D-03 — fuels and PCT-management discussion
Status: Queued. Proposal for review: interpret phase-specific fuel conditions and the matched woody contrast as linked silvicultural, fuels, and fire-management information. Keep the distinction between inferred potential surface-fuel contribution and direct slash measurement explicit.
Review product: 1.5–2-page subsection. Acceptance test: it does not presume one downstream fire-modeling use or extend beyond the reviewed design.


D-04 — limits, integration, and future work
Status: Queued. Proposal for review: close the Discussion with the limitations that constrain the regeneration and fuel interpretations, then identify targeted future work without reopening detailed model results.
Review product: 0.5–1-page subsection. Acceptance test: it resolves rather than repeats caveats from prior discussion subsections.

title: Publication workflow and review queue
text:
Introduction, supplement, and closing matter

I-01 — management problem and study purpose
Status: Queued — after Discussion. Proposal for review: condense the multiaged-silviculture framing to establish the management problem, then state the study purpose and scope as supported by the accepted Results/Discussion.


I-02 — regeneration and retention context
Status: Queued — after Discussion. Proposal for review: retain only the sprouting, light, and retention context needed to motivate D-01/D-02; move broad background not needed for the study question out of the main text.


I-03 — fuels context and questions
Status: Queued — after Discussion. Proposal for review: merge and focus fuel context on phase-specific reference conditions and the PCT question; avoid broad fire-management claims unsupported by the study.
Review product for I-01–I-03: a 4–5-page Introduction with a final, aligned study-purpose paragraph. Acceptance test: its questions are each answered by an accepted Results subsection.


S-01 — supplement and machine-readable outputs
Status: Queued — after main displays. Proposal for review: inventory every item excluded from the main text: detailed model registry, diagnostics, pairwise comparisons, optional Douglas-fir detail, expanded fuel components, and machine-readable phase-specific values. Link each item from its accepted main-text counterpart.


C-01 — conclusions
Status: Queued — after Discussion. Proposal for review: write a short conclusion limited to the management implications directly supported by the accepted regeneration, sprout, and fuel results.


A-01 — abstract and title
Status: Queued — last. Proposal for review: draft the abstract from the accepted results, methods, discussion, and conclusion; set the final title only after the abstract has stabilized. This preserves the backwards-writing sequence above.
